title: Chemical selection and runoff boundaries
audience: Trainee or new worker on the window cleaning (all heights) track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Identify safety and authorisation decisions associated with chemical selection and runoff boundaries.
Explain the applicable risk hierarchy and specialist responsibilities for chemical selection and runoff boundaries.
Produce a defensible stop-work, competent-person referral or restricted handover using mock evidence.

instruction.heading: Where this lesson sits
instruction.body: This lesson is part of the window cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level work, water-fed pole work and elevated access work on glazing and frames. Work above ground level, or work from a ladder, scaffold or elevating work platform, is restricted. It needs written employer authorisation under a site-specific risk assessment, and the worker must hold any licence the state or territory requires for the equipment used. Safe Work Australia's working-heights page sets the high-risk construction threshold at a fall of more than 2 metres. South Australia lowered its threshold from 3 metres to 2 metres, effective 1 July 2026. This lesson is a desk-based drill. It does not give permission to apply any product on a real site.

instruction.heading: Product approval and the label
instruction.body: Every product used on a job must be on the approved list for that job, and it must be used exactly as its label directs. Before a product is used, read the label and find its safety data sheet (SDS). Workers who use or handle a hazardous chemical must be able to reach its SDS easily, and a business with hazardous chemicals at the workplace should hold an SDS for each one. A hazardous chemicals register lists those chemicals with their current SDS and is kept where workers can reach it. If a container has no label, or the SDS is not on site, the product is not used. Record the gap and report it. A product that is approved for one surface is not approved for every surface, and a product that is approved for one purpose is not approved for a different one. Use the label's list of surfaces and its directions as the limit, not the habit of the person holding the bottle.

instruction.heading: Surface compatibility
instruction.body: A product that is safe on one glazing frame may damage another. Window frames can be aluminium, timber, painted or coated, or made of a plastic that clouds or softens. Seals and sealants can swell, lift or discolour. Glass can be etched by the wrong product, and a coating can be stripped. Surface compatibility is checked against the label, the manufacturer's guidance and the method approval, and then confirmed with a test on a sample area that the site has released for testing. In this desk lesson the test is planned on paper only. Record the surfaces the product is approved for, the surfaces it is not approved for, and the test that is needed before any use. Do not treat a product as compatible because it looks similar to one that worked before.

instruction.heading: Runoff: where the water goes
instruction.body: Runoff is the water and product that leaves the surface and flows away. The question is always where it goes. In Queensland, a council page on water pressure cleaning says that the wastewater is a prescribed water contaminant that must not enter roadside gutters or stormwater systems, and that letting it do so is unlawful under the state's Environmental Protection Act. The same page describes ways to capture the water, such as sending it to a garden or to a holding tank for collection by a licensed liquid waste contractor, and warns that a drain must be protected from the water. That guidance is for Queensland and for that council.

instruction.heading: Landscaped drains and the lesson case
instruction.body: The lesson case is an alkaline cleaning product proposed for use above landscaped runoff drains, without product approval. Treat any drain as connected to stormwater until the site confirms otherwise, and keep the product and the wash water off drains, gutters, garden beds, plantings and neighbouring property. Do not test the product over a drain to see how it reacts. The first safe action is to hold the product. Tell the site controller, ask for the approved product for that surface and area, and ask for written runoff controls. If no control is approved, the chemical use does not go ahead. The site controller decides whether a different method, which does not use the product, is used instead. That decision is theirs, not the cleaner's.

instruction.heading: Role boundaries and the stop-work decision
instruction.body: Hold chemical use until the site confirms surface compatibility, the product's instructions and the runoff controls. General cleaning training does not sign off rope descent, platform operation, anchor certification, electrical clearance or emergency rescue capability. A trainee who finds that one of these is needed must refer it. The stop-work rule applies whenever the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; when wind, rain, ice or fading light changes the conditions; when exposed wiring, damaged cable or water near electrical equipment is seen or suspected; when a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; when the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or when you are asked to work above ground level without the required licence or authorisation. Stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming.

instruction.heading: Protective equipment is the last control
instruction.body: Safe Work Australia's risk-management code places containment, elimination, substitution, isolation and engineering controls above personal protective equipment, and describes PPE as a last resort or a back-up to higher controls. The right order here is to keep the product off the drain, to use the approved product only, and to use the least product that works, and then to wear the gloves and eye protection the SDS sets. PPE does not make a drain safe to receive a product.

instruction.heading: Records and communication
instruction.body: Record the product name, the label check, the SDS reference, the surfaces the product is and is not approved for, the drain and garden map notes, the decision reached, the person told, and the time. Use the same observation, inference and approval separation as the other lessons in this track. Do not write that a product is safe for an area unless the label, the SDS and the written approval all say so.

instruction.heading: Licence and height notes
instruction.body: A boom-type elevating work platform needs a WP high risk work licence where its boom is 11 metres or more in New South Wales, Western Australia, Tasmania and the Northern Territory. In Queensland, a shorter boom may not need it, because the Queensland definition does not cover platforms shorter than 11 metres. The Victorian WP class has no boom-length threshold, so the licence is not limited by length there. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. The national model code uses the 11-metre threshold, measured from the original design. Scissor lifts need no high risk work licence in Victoria, and the Northern Territory requires the operator to be competent. Completing this lesson is not a licence, certificate or authority for regulated work.

instruction.heading: Electrical notice
instruction.body: This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. In NSW, electrical wiring work includes repairing and altering an installation and needs a licence or certificate. Victorian rules on PV work could not be read in this pass. Treat all panels and cables as live, and refer any electrical fault to a licensed electrician.

instruction.heading: Trainer-led tabletop practice
instruction.body: Create a simulated product-and-drainage review sheet using fictitious container labels, SDS excerpts and a drawn drain and garden map. Use photographs, drawn plans, fictitious work orders and inert desk materials only. Trainer checks each entry for accuracy and intervenes if the learner proposes unauthorised real-world activity, including any test over a real drain.

procedure: Identify the product from its label, and confirm the label and the SDS are both on site and that the product is on the approved list.
Confirm the surfaces and the purpose the product is approved for, and note any surface it is not approved for.
Map the drains, gutters, garden beds, plantings and neighbouring property that the runoff could reach.
Decide the runoff control with the site controller. If no control is approved, hold the chemical use.
Record the product check, the drain map notes, the decision and the person told.
Use the product only after written approval, within the label directions, and stop if runoff reaches a drain or a garden.

workedExamples.situation: An alkaline cleaning product is proposed for a facade where the runoff would run over landscaped drains, and the product has no approval for that use.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the first safe action, and who must be told?
workedExamples.reasoning: Hold the product and do not use it, and do not test it over the drains. Tell the site controller, and record the time and the name of the person told. Ask for an approved product for the surface and area, and for written runoff controls. Map the drains and the landscaping on the record sheet. If no control is approved, the chemical use does not go ahead, and the site controller decides whether a different method is used.

workedExamples.situation: A stain on a coated aluminium frame does not respond to the approved product, and a worker suggests a stronger product from the van.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do, and what do you write?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not use the stronger product. The approved product sets the limit for the surface. Record that the stain did not respond, the surface, and the product used. Ask the site controller for an approved alternative in writing, and do not use any product that is not on the approved list until that approval is recorded.

workedExamples.situation: A worker finds a spray bottle with no label in the van, and the SDS for the job's product is not in the folder.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the status of the bottle and of the job?
workedExamples.reasoning: The bottle is not used, and it is set aside and reported. The job cannot use a chemical whose label and SDS are not available, so the chemical part of the work is held. Record the gap, the time and the person told, and ask for the SDS to be placed on site before the work resumes.

equipmentAndPpe: Fictitious container labels and SDS excerpts (desk materials only).
Drawn drain, gutter and garden map with a notes column.
Approved product list for the job (see business field), with surfaces and purposes marked.
Runoff record sheet with decision, hold and person-told fields.
For any future real site: PPE is set by the SDS and the risk assessment, and runoff controls are approved by the site controller. Neither is used in this desk lesson.

commonErrors.error: Using a product that is approved for one surface on a different surface.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the label's surface list and the method approval before each product is used.

commonErrors.error: Using a product because it is commonly used in cleaning.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only the approved product for the job, and check its label and SDS.

commonErrors.error: Assuming runoff goes to the sewer.
commonErrors.prevention: Treat drains as stormwater until the site confirms the route, and hold the work if it is unknown.

commonErrors.error: Testing a product over a drain to see how it reacts.
commonErrors.prevention: Test only on an area the site has released for testing, and never over a drain.

commonErrors.error: Using a stronger product after the approved one fails.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, record the result, and request an approved alternative in writing.

commonErrors.error: Relying on PPE to make runoff safe.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep the product off the drain first; PPE is the last control.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Chemicals and SDS. Safe Work Australia's guidance says that the SDS must be easy for workers who use or handle the chemical to reach. The hazardous chemicals register must list each hazardous chemical with its current SDS, and must be kept where workers can reach it. Products are used under their labels.

Runoff. In Queensland, a council page states that pressure-cleaning wastewater must not enter roadside gutters or stormwater systems, and that doing so is unlawful under the Environmental Protection Act 1994.

Licence and height notice. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height, on roofs, from elevated work platforms, or on solar systems, and it is not a licence, certificate or authority for regulated work. The licence thresholds for boom-type platforms are set out in the instruction above. Check the rule in your state or territory and obtain written employer authorisation before any work above ground level.

Stop-work rule. Stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

Electrical notice. This lesson does not grant the right to work on, isolate or repair solar (PV) systems or any electrical installation. NSW electrical wiring work includes repairing and altering an installation.

Control order. Safe Work Australia's risk-management code places PPE at the lowest level of control, as a last resort or a back-up (copy dated December 2011, section 4.1; a later edition was not read).

qualityStandard: Product label, SDS and approval are each checked separately, and the gap is recorded where one is missing.
Surface compatibility is checked against the label and the method approval, and any test is planned and approved before use.
Runoff controls are confirmed by the site before any product is used, and drains are treated as stormwater until the route is confirmed.
No unapproved product is used near drains, gutters or landscaping, and the trainer-led practice uses fictitious labels, SDS excerpts and drawn plans only.
documentationEvidence: Product record: name, label check, SDS reference and approved surfaces.
Drain and garden map with the runoff decision and the person told.
Hold or stop record where a product was not used, with the reason.
summary: Check the product against its label, its SDS and the approved list before use, and keep it to the surfaces it is approved for.
Treat runoff over drains and landscaping as a product-approval question, and do not use an alkaline product there without written approval.
This is a paper drill with made-up container labels and safety data extracts, and it grants no right to apply any product on a real site.

knowledgeChecks.question: For chemical selection and runoff boundaries, what evidence must be established before allocating work, and which facts are still unverified?
options: The product's name, because it is commonly used in cleaning and is well known across the trade and the industry today
Trying a product over the drains to see how it reacts with the water and the grime on the site
Product-label verification, surface compatibility and runoff controls, confirmed by the site before any chemical use
Confirmation that the runoff can go to the landscaped drains and the gardens next to the building

knowledgeChecks.question: Runoff from a cleaning job is heading toward a drain. What is correct?
options: Let it flow, because it is only water and it will dry out soon on the path, the drive, the lawn and the steps
Stop and contain it using the site's approved controls, and check that the product is approved for that area
Add more product so that it is diluted before it reaches the drain, the gutter and the grate

knowledgeChecks.question: A product has no safety data sheet on site. What is correct?
options: Use it, because the label is enough to show how to use it safely
Do not use it until the SDS is available and read, and report the gap
Use only a small amount, so the risk is small on the site today
